rationale: Lycopolitan reflex of Greek κολυμβητής 'diver, pearl-diver.' Regular Lyc. ⲭ for κ; -ⲗⲕⲙ̄ⲥⲉ from -λυμβ-ητ-. Central image of the pearl-diving parable in this kephalaion: the diver descends into the sea to retrieve pearls from oyster shells, allegorically the apostle who descends into the world to retrieve souls from the flesh.

Native Coptic compound for the pearl-bearing mollusk. Likely related to ⲙⲟⲩ 'water' + a creature-element. The shell of the oyster (ⲡⲭⲉⲕ / ⲧⲁⲭⲗⲉ) is what the diver breaks to extract the pearl. In the parable's interpretation, the oyster represents the flesh-host of the soul.

Lycopolitan plural of ϣⲁⲧⲉ 'pit, well, depth.' In this kephalaion, the wells of the sea where the divers go to find pearls — typologically the cosmic luminaries (ⲙ̄ⲫⲱⲥⲧⲏⲣ, sun and moon) where souls are gathered before being conveyed to the Aeons of Greatness.

Hapax in this corpus. Paired with ⲧⲃⲏⲧⲉ 'date-palm' as the two natural exempla to which the flesh of humanity is likened in the parable. The functional sense in the typology requires a host/casing term — probably the shell of the oyster. Etymology unclear; possibly cognate with a Lyc. term for shell or fruit-pod. Confidence moderate.

Possibly Greek θήκη 'case, sheath' adapted to Lycopolitan, with ⲗ for η/κ unusual but possible. The 'casing of the oyster' is what the divers must break or open to retrieve the pearl, allegorically the violent act of releasing the soul from the flesh. Confidence moderate.

Greek loanword ἁρπαγή 'snatching, plundering' with Lyc. ⲍ-onset (regular for Greek words beginning in spiritus or rough breathing). Used here in cognate-object construction with ⲧⲱⲣⲡ̄ 'snatch' (in glossary): 'the plundering which they snatch.' The act of snatching the pearl from the oyster, allegorically the deliverance of the soul.

Greek ἀρχιέμπορος 'chief merchant, head of merchant guild.' Capitalized here as a divine cosmic title: the great Chief-Merchant to whom the diver-apostles deliver the retrieved pearl-souls. Coordinates with the merchant-typology established in earlier kephalaia (cf. ⲡⲉϩⲛⲁⲃ ⲛⲉⲟⲩⲉⲓⲛ, ⲙⲛⲧⲓⲉⲡϣⲱⲧ in accumulated vocabulary).

Greek loanword τύχη 'fortune, fate, allotted lot.' Used here naturalistically of the diver's varying success per his fate, paired with ⲡⲉⲧⲧⲏϣ ⲛⲉϩ 'what is appointed to him' (Coptic equivalent). Standard.

Lycopolitan qualitative meaning 'sharp, cutting.' Likely cognate with ⲧⲱⲃⲥ̄ 'sharpen, point' or ⲥⲱⲧⲡ̄ in its 'sharpened' sense. Used in the chapter 81 heading of Wisdom 'sharp in tongue' more than the sword.

Homograph of accumulated ⲡⲥⲁⲡ 'the time, the appointed turn.' In Kephalaion 81 (this page, lines 26 and 33) ⲡⲥⲁⲡ clearly means 'sword' — Lycopolitan/dialectal reflex of Sahidic ⲥⲏϥⲉ. Distinguished by context: comparative construction 'sharper than the X' demands 'sword,' and Hebrews 4:12 supplies the well-known intertextual model. Important to flag the polysemy in future occurrences.

Lycopolitan ⲧⲱⲃⲍ̄ = Sahidic ⲧⲱⲃϩ̄ 'pray, beseech, entreat' (regular ⲍ for ϩ). Used as Coptic 1sg present in disciple's petition formula 'I beseech you, my Lord, that you make known...' Standard Kephalaia dialogue opener.
Lycopolitan reflex of Sahidic ⲗⲁⲥ 'tongue.' Vowel-shift ⲁ→ⲉ in unstressed position. Used in the chapter heading 'sharp in tongue' (i.e., sharp in speech/utterance).

Variant of accumulated tentative ⲡⲱⲓⲭⲍ 'abyss, pit.' The compound -ⲭⲍϩ̄ may incorporate a deepening-suffix or be a Lyc. orthographic expansion. Designates the deep sea from which pearls are retrieved by the diver — cosmological correspondent of the depths from which souls are raised.
